The mechanism by which an airplane wing generates lift is a fascinating intersection of fluid dynamics and Newtonian mechanics. While popular culture often simplifies this process into a single rule, the reality is a complex interplay of several physical principles working in concert. To fully understand how lift is produced, we must look beyond simple explanations and examine the interaction between the wing’s shape, its angle of attack, and the surrounding air.

The most common, yet incomplete, explanation is the "equal transit time" theory, which suggests that air traveling over the curved top of the wing must move faster than air traveling underneath to meet at the trailing edge simultaneously. While it is true that air moves faster over the top surface, the "equal transit" premise is physically incorrect; the air particles do not need to meet at the same time. Instead, the primary driver of this speed difference is the curvature of the wing and the angle at which it is pitched relative to the oncoming airflow, known as the angle of attack.

According to Bernoulli’s Principle, as the velocity of a fluid increases, its static pressure decreases. Because the wing is angled and curved, it forces the air above it to accelerate. This acceleration creates a region of lower pressure above the wing compared to the higher pressure
